fixes.explanation: Paul says it just like that: "The death He died, He died to sin once for all…" (Romans 6:10). It's finished. No repeat, no encore. Once for all means the one time was enough.

Paul, the apostle, asks that question, but he doesn't say yes to it. His very next words are "Certainly not!" (Romans 6:2). That's like dumping a whole bowl of dough on the floor and asking, "Shall I do it again so I get better at cleaning?" Nobody says, "Great idea, do it again."

Law is a word Paul does use in this passage, but not here. In verse 2 his reason is that believers "…died to sin…" Law shows up later, when he says they are "…not under law, but under grace." (Romans 6:14). So this answer is close to the neighborhood, but it's a different house.

Right there in verse 6: "…that we should no longer be slaves to sin." The old self was crucified with Christ so that "…the body of sin might be rendered powerless…" Paul's point is that believers are no longer slaves to sin.

Counting it by the year is a fair guess, but Paul doesn't give that kind of count. Verse 10 says, "The death He died, He died to sin once for all…" Once for all is the number to hold onto. And right after that, he says the life Christ lives, He lives to God.
